iterations.theme: Introduction, the guest's credibility, the significance of the expert paper on nutrition in professional cycling, and carbohydrate intake on a ride

sections.subtitle: The guide, the paper from 2016 to 2025, and a guest who goes back to the couch
sections.screenshot_description: Host Josip greets the viewers and announces the guest Luka Batur and the cyclist nutrition guide
sections.content:
Josip opens the episode with a greeting to the viewers and an announcement of the guest, Luka Batur, who is appearing on the channel for the third time, and for the second time on his own. Before the topic itself, Josip draws attention to the cyclist nutrition guide that Batur wrote. The guide covers why nutrition is important in cycling, the roles of fats, carbohydrates and proteins, how many carbohydrates to eat on a single ride, what nutrition looks like in everyday training, and what to eat before a ride, during it and after it. Those interested can find it via the first link in the video description. Josip admits that the announcement sounds a bit like an advertisement, and Batur adds that he tried to be honest toward the viewers.

Batur says he is always glad to come, and Josip reminds him that his first appearance was in one of the earlier podcasts, after which many questions remained unanswered. They will stay aside this time, because today's topic is special.

The main occasion for the conversation is the recently published **most comprehensive review of nutrition in professional cycling**, which Batur sent to Josip. According to Josip's description, the authors analyzed the period from 2016 to 2025, and nutritionists from two professional teams and from one university took part in the paper. The goal of the episode is, through the examples of Batur and Josip's "modest examples" and through the viewers' questions, to translate this expert material into the language of an ordinary rider.

sections.subtitle: Who is Luka Batur: from the chemistry of metabolism to triathlon
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur presents his education and experience working with athletes
sections.content:
To Josip's question of why the audience should listen to him at all, Batur answers that his credibility always sounds a little arrogant and that this is judged by clients and colleagues. He states the facts as follows: **he is a master of nutrition**, and he graduated from the Faculty of Food Technology and Biotechnology of the University of Zagreb. He emphasizes that it was not a course or a weekend education, but long and detailed schooling with a lot of chemistry and biochemistry.

That background, he claims, is the difference compared to self-proclaimed experts. He says that in practice it is often accepted that someone is an expert because they "have been eating for a long time" or have been riding a bike for a long time, so "what is some nerd going to tell me". Knowing human metabolism, including the field of sports nutrition from which the papers under discussion come, gives, in his opinion, a level more.

After university, Batur works at KBC Zagreb, and besides that he works with amateur and professional athletes and with people who have diagnoses and have to correct their diet. He has been in triathlon, he says, since the last years of his undergraduate studies, approximately since 2017, and he graduated in 2021, so he is also on two wheels. His approach is to polish the "scientific expert picture" with what he sees in the field and what is achievable for people, because "science is one thing, and practice another".

sections.subtitle: What has changed since college: fewer new facts, a better approach to athletes
sections.screenshot_description: Batur explains how his approach to athletes has changed over the years
sections.content:
Josip asks how much Batur learned after university through courses, books and work itself. The guest answers that he did not get many more scientific facts than at university, because science basically has not changed drastically. What he, as he says, **has certainly advanced in** is the way of shaping information for end users, clients and athletes.

He admits that over time he also changed some things he had advocated earlier. "I'm not ashamed to say, back then I was a fool", he says, explaining that at the beginning he did not have all the information in his hands and that today he works differently than right after university.

He improves his expertise regularly. Two years ago he was in Manchester with a fellow nutritionist, where he listened live to the authors of the papers under discussion here. Seminars on cyclists' strategies, which come directly from institutes connected with the Tour, are rare and paid, and whoever wants to follow them has to know where to look. Batur says he was pleased when, at those lectures, he realized that he was finding his way well in what he heard.

sections.subtitle: The secrets of professional teams and "marginal gains" in nutrition science
sections.screenshot_description: Batur explains why teams keep new discoveries secret, and Josip compares bikes and small details
sections.content:
Batur explains that it is not a single paper, but **six or seven related papers** that are summarized in order to give people simpler, condensed information. At the same time, he is sure that professional teams also have secrets that the head nutritionist does not simply spill. One of his unrealized plans is to work once as a nutritionist in some professional team, where, he says, he would have something to learn from older and more expert colleagues.

Josip adds that cycling carries the stigma of doping, which unfortunately is also tied to nutrition science and doctors. Still, he emphasizes that he does not necessarily mean doping, but the **collection of small advantages** that teams seek over their opponents.

Batur agrees and stresses that the authors of the papers are scientists who are at the same time top practitioners, and teams do not employ just anyone. One of the authors, as he describes him, is responsible for the well-known figures on glucose and fructose intake (60 and 90 grams), and was frustrated that this information did not reach the field as much as he wanted. The paper was probably in preparation for two years before publication, and if something truly revolutionary appears, it is probably kept secret, because teams compete with each other. As an example he states that a rider after the Tour posts on social media only how many carbohydrates he ate, while the real details are many more.

Josip continues this thought with an example from his own experience: with Domagoj in Decathlon he saw a top bike on display and concluded that there is almost no difference between top bikes. Professionals probably train similarly, and the difference is made by the **sum of micro-details**: a little bike, a little nutrition science, a little training, along with talent.

sections.subtitle: Authors, universities and teams: who stands behind the paper
sections.screenshot_description: Batur lists the authors of the paper and their teams and universities
sections.content:
To Josip's question of who the authors are and why the paper is so important, Batur says there are several of them. One, according to his recollection, was for many years the head nutritionist of the Jumbo-Visma team, and is currently, he thinks, the nutritionist of another team. He invites viewers to correct him in the comments if he said something wrong. Among the authors he also mentions **James Morton**, whom he listened to live at a congress two years ago. Morton is a nutritionist, but also works in the world of football, and Batur, joking, retells to the audience where that expert used to go in football clubs. He also mentions an Australian scientist, whose name is not reliably recorded in the transcript, so we do not state it here. All of them are, he says, the "cream" of nutrition science.

He also told an anecdote from that congress: he was surprised by how **critical of one another** scientists are and how openly they tell each other that they are wrong. One year they published a paper on relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S), that is, on whether energy deficiency leads to fractures and injuries, which caused a lot of controversy among athletes. The following year at the same congress there was a lecture on the programme with a direct response, in a lively debate in which the authors were called out. Despite that, those authors collaborate on new papers. Batur thinks that this does not exist in Croatia: criticism is quickly paid for with a block, and he himself says he is blocked on several profiles because he pointed out the shortcomings of some paper.

The papers are **open access**, so anyone can read them, and the links will be in the podcast description. Their significance lies in the fact that they summarize all the research conducted so far on cyclists and add experiences from practice, which are marked in the text as "personal observation". Batur therefore regards it as a paper that will for some time remain the **"bible"** for experts who want to get acquainted with nutrition in this sport.

sections.subtitle: Revolution or unified knowledge? Batur looks for the right epithet
sections.screenshot_description: Batur explains that the paper is a comprehensive overview, not a revolution
sections.content:
Josip announces that the goal of the conversation will be to bring the topic down to the level of the average person, even his own, and to compare the expert material with the amateur and recreational world, from gran fondo riders to those who ride only for their own pleasure. He asks whether there has ever been a similar paper before and whether this one brings anything revolutionary.

Batur answers that "revolutionary" is the wrong epithet. It is more accurate to say that knowledge that already existed has been **unified in one place** and in a handy format. As an example he cites glycogen supercompensation, about which there are papers from the 1960s that are still valid today. There were also earlier recommendations on carbohydrates in training and competition, but this paper was commissioned with the idea that several experts from several different teams give their review of individual topics in one place. It is best described as a **"comprehensive review"**, and Batur adds that it "hammered a nail into the coffin" of some dilemmas.

Looking at it, he noticed a few things he had not taken into account earlier, but most were known. He warns, however, that what is banal to him is not necessarily banal to laypeople and athletes in the field. He sees special value in the open approach, because quite a few papers are closed and available only through an institution or for payment.

sections.subtitle: What the paper contains: from intake on the ride to the kitchen on the move
sections.screenshot_description: Batur lists the topics the paper covers: intake on the ride, periodization, recovery, supplements
sections.content:
Josip asks what exactly the paper contains. He mentions data on the average caloric expenditure of cyclists, a graph of the growth of average speeds in races (races are faster and faster today) and the famous figure of **120 grams of carbohydrates per hour**. He adds that he was recently amazed by the speeds in the finale of one Giro stage.

Batur lists the content:

- **Intake during the ride**: the figures and their differences depending on the stage and terrain are covered in detail. Examples from practice show that 120 grams per hour is not the standard for every stage and every cyclist, so in places on flat, shorter stages they take in even 50 grams less per hour, while on mountain stages it goes up to 100 and more. The paper also gives a broader context on when to go higher and when it is not necessary.
- **Periodization of nutrition** depending on the level of preparation and the time of year.
- **Injuries and athletes' health**, a topic that is rarely talked about.
- **Recovery**, not only after a single training session, but from day to day and from month to month. Batur notes that the average professional, roughly, competes about 80 days a year, while he trains the remaining 250 and more days, and that part of the year often passes "under the radar".
- **Supplements**: which ones work, which are nonsense, and which are potentially dangerous.
- **Sport food**: the differences between factory gels, liquids and bars, and athletes' preferences.
- **The kitchen**: one of the related papers, "From Play to Performance", deals with the cooperation of nutritionists and chefs. One paper is even dedicated to the kitchen bus, that is, the teams' mobile kitchens, in which the chef translates the figures from the nutritionist's plan into something edible on a plate.

Batur concludes that "absolutely everything" is covered, so the paper truly deserves the name of a bible. Josip follows up on this with a personal anecdote about meeting the Jumbo-Visma team at a training camp on Rogla, when they helped him fix his glasses, and he in Rogla did not know that the lens in them can be replaced.

sections.subtitle: Why one takes in 50 and another 120 grams: carbohydrates as rocket fuel
sections.screenshot_description: Batur explains that intensity and volume determine carbohydrate intake
sections.content:
Josip has prepared a series of questions: why one rider takes in 50 and another 120 grams, whether it depends on digestive abilities or on stores before the race, and why some choose gels and some bars. Batur starts from the basics. He notes that amateurs and recreational riders, seeing how much professionals take in, often imitate those figures because an impression is created of "the more the better and the faster I'll cross the finish line", and that without thinking about context.

When Josip tests him with a question about the role of carbohydrates, Batur simplifies: carbohydrates are **"rocket fuel"**. Among all the athletes he works with, from water polo players and tennis players to runners, he has not yet met a single one who eats enough carbohydrates. Intake, according to him, should primarily be dictated by **intensity**, then by **volume**, that is, by needs: how much is being expended, how hard the pedals are being pressed and what the demands of the training or race are. A six-hour stage with 4000 meters of climbing cannot be compared with a flat stage.

A practical example: if someone rides a training session of an hour and fifteen minutes, there is no point in cramming 120 grams into it. A Sunday group ride of about a hundred kilometers with some twenty people, where one rides in shelter, can end with an average power of only about 150 W over five hours. Batur says: "It's great if you can take in 120 grams per hour without diarrhea, but the question is whether you need it." The paper does not claim that 120 grams per hour automatically means reaching the finish line faster, because performance is a much broader picture than how much someone "managed to cram in".

He is partly glad that the paper has raised athletes' awareness, because on the weekend rides of his triathlon club he used to see intake from zero to 30 grams per hour. Still, the figure of 120 should not be the ultimate goal. He estimates that **80 to 90 percent of those who ride three to five times a week**, with two harder rides of two and a half to three and a half hours, would be fine within a range of roughly 60 to 90 grams per hour, and often lower. Few people sustain high intensity for long, so the great majority of recreational riders have no sense chasing extreme intakes either.

sections.subtitle: Recreational rider, semi-amateur and the fuel tank: how much to think about intake
sections.screenshot_description: Batur advises recreational riders to eat regularly and by feel, and compares the body with a car and a tank
sections.content:
Josip introduces himself as a "heavy recreational rider" whose range is the brevet, while he describes his friend Domagoj as a semi-amateur who goes to gran fondo events. He asks whether and how much one should count carbohydrates, add them up and gradually, over the course of a year, raise intake from 30 to 80-90 grams.

Batur notices the key sentence: Josip said that his performances are "non-existent". If it does not matter how fast he will cross the finish line, **there is no need to take pen in hand and add things up**, but that does not mean going without a care either. It is in the rider's interest that those few hours with the group are a pleasure. Hypoglycemia in the sense of fainting on the bike is rare. The best advice for such a rider is to go "by feel", but to eat **regularly**: for example, a bar per hour or one bidon with something sweeter. The recommendation for continuous intake still stands, so that it does not happen that someone, after two and a half hours on a 200-kilometer brevet, realizes that their pockets are still full.

For the average recreational rider, "a bar per hour" maintains a normal level of speed and power, and whoever wants to press the pedals harder must also take in more, because a harder effort means greater expenditure and faster emptying of stores. Batur illustrates this with a comparison with a car: for a short drive to Zaprešić one can go on reserve, but if one has to get to Dubrovnik by eight in the evening, one must know how much fuel fits in the tank and where the next gas station is (or charging station for those who drive on electricity). The more serious the demands, the more one has to take care of **what, how much and when** one eats.

sections.subtitle: Žumberak and the "blockage": what happens when you eat too late
sections.screenshot_description: Josip retells a ride to Žumberak on which he ate too late and felt a blockage
sections.content:
Josip retells his recent example: a strenuous recreational ride with two big climbs to Žumberak, one of which lasted about ten kilometers. The day before he was busy, so in a hurry he bought whatever he found first. In his pockets he had a sandwich he had made himself, a bar of about 500 calories that is hard to eat on the ride, a gel, a chocolate bar and Haribo gummy candies. For the first two and a half hours he ate nothing, which had never happened to him before: some things he was saving "for something", and the bar was too heavy for him to eat on a climb. Only at the top did he eat the sandwich. Since he had put off eating, he became hungry and suddenly ate several sweets from his pocket, after which a **"blockage"** set in: a feeling that he would eat more, but with mild nausea and an inability to continue riding. He assumes he suddenly took in a large number of grams of carbohydrates that he was not used to. Fortunately, there were no digestive problems.

Batur answers that such unwanted events can be explained by science, and then immediately moves on to the question about the choice of gels, bars and candies. At a more intense pace, when riding in a group and it is hard to take a hand off the handlebars, and the pulse is close to 170, it is impossible to chew. The priority is therefore **fluids and gels**, while bars are reserved for calmer parts. To more advanced amateurs he advises looking at the profile of the course and eating food that takes longer to chew in a calmer part of the route, not at the start of a climb.

sections.subtitle: Why no fats, proteins and fiber: how fuel reaches the muscles fastest
sections.screenshot_description: Batur explains that fats, proteins and fiber slow down gastric emptying
sections.content:
On solid food on the ride, Batur stresses that all the papers, this one included, are very clear: a bar should have as little fat, protein and fiber as possible. It is wanted that, although solid, it be as a rule **almost pure carbohydrate**. The reason is simple: fats, proteins and fiber **slow down gastric emptying and digestion**, that is, the transit of glucose from the stomach into the intestines, and later from the intestines into the bloodstream. In race conditions or intense training, the goal is for fuel to reach the blood as soon as possible, and from the blood into the muscles.

Josip adds that in such conditions "you have to get to Dubrovnik". Batur confirms and makes a distinction: when going on a so-called "coffee ride" and there is no intensity, it does not matter what is eaten, what matters is that it is tasty and that it is eaten. But as soon as one enters intense training or a race, one must take care of the physiological side and the ratio of macronutrients. For that reason **he does not recommend protein bars during a ride or race**, for two reasons:

- proteins are not a significant source of energy,
- there is no need to fear a drop in muscle mass, because the most important thing for it is the total daily protein intake, not what is eaten on the ride. Proteins can be taken in after training or the race, however long it lasted.

sections.subtitle: Start early: the digestive system under stress and the "eat for tomorrow" rule
sections.screenshot_description: Batur explains why intake should start within the first twenty or so minutes of the ride
sections.content:
Batur returns to Josip's story and says that it was a mistake not to eat in the first two hours. As the ride or race goes on, the athlete is more and more tired and intensity often rises. **Most of the blood is directed toward the extremities**, so the digestive system and the stomach are partly "shortchanged". The brain, he says, does not send blood to the stomach when the legs are producing 1600 watts and need oxygen and nutrients. Weaker blood supply to the digestive system means weaker contractions and mixing, and thus poorer digestion.

That is why he advises athletes to start intake as early as possible, while the digestive system is still maximally functional and not under stress. In that way digestive troubles are avoided and as many nutrients as possible are brought into the bloodstream in the first part of the activity. Batur notes that amateurs often make a mistake: they wait an hour and fifteen minutes and only then take out a gel. He himself, when he knows he is going on a hard ride or a gran fondo, takes the first gel already after some fifteen to twenty minutes.

Josip connects this with his own motto **"eat for tomorrow"**, that is, eat for what awaits you in an hour. He adds that he also says this in examples from his bike-packing trips, which are not so demanding, but on which one must also eat in advance. He announces that he is interested in a few more things, among them how the researchers arrived at the famous figures of 120 grams per hour.

iterations.theme: The physiology of carbohydrate absorption, alternatives to gels, injury prevention through nutrition, and an example of nutrition at a gran fondo

sections.subtitle: How the figure of 120 grams was arrived at: isotopes, glucose infusion and the „barrier“ in the gut
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains the experiment with glucose infusion and the conclusion that the barrier to absorption is in the digestive system
sections.content:
To close the first part of the conversation, Josip asks Luka Batur something that particularly interested him: how scientists even arrived at the famous figure of 120 grams of carbohydrates per hour and why precisely at it.

Luka explains that the method is actually very interesting. The carbohydrate, that is, the solution the athlete drinks, is **labeled with a special isotope**. After that, with the help of masks and indirect calorimetry, the amount of labeled carbon dioxide is measured in the exhaled air. If it is known how much glucose was taken in and how much labeled CO2 was exhaled, it can be calculated how much of it the body actually used. According to Luka's words, a similar type of test is today also done by colleagues in Ljubljana.

Scientists then carried out various tests and looked for where the barrier is, that is, how much at most the muscle can utilize. At one point they gave a cyclist a **glucose infusion**. Luka stresses that something like that cannot be done in real conditions, but it was interesting for the researchers to see what happens when glucose is taken in directly into the blood. The result was clear: everything injected directly into the blood enters the cell and is used up. From this they concluded that the **limit lies not in the muscle, but somewhere in the digestive system**, that is, at the level of the intestine.

Luka explains this vividly as **"toll booths"** at a toll station:

- glucose enters the bloodstream through one transporter (passage),
- fructose enters through an entirely different transporter.

Research with the labeled isotope showed that the limit for glucose alone is about **60 grams per hour**. When fructose was added, which uses other transporters, the total amount could be raised further, so more fuel is delivered into the bloodstream. Luka sums up that it is actually a matter of **the physiology of the gut**, not of the muscle. Josip comments that he finds it interesting that this can even be measured.

sections.subtitle: Ordinary sugar, glucose, honey or gummy candies: should one buy expensive gels at all?
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur answers a viewer's question about replacing gels with sugar and honey
sections.content:
Josip reads a viewer's question (Mr. Brko): what does Luka think about replacing expensive gels and sports drinks with ordinary sugar with a little salt, given that ordinary sugar has a glucose-to-fructose ratio of 50:50 and no unnecessary flavorings or other additives. Another viewer follows up with a question about honey.

Luka answers that they have researched that too. They compared different sugars, among them glucose alone, fructose alone and even lactose. The idea was to compare their physical properties in the gut. Fructose can cause **a little more chaos in the gut**, and ordinary white sugar (sucrose) contains precisely glucose and fructose. Luka stresses that gels **really do not need to be bought** and that many people have found another way. He himself, in his student days, when he had no money for ready-made products, bought glucose in a drugstore and mixed it into drinks. That is why he would **give a slight advantage to glucose** over ordinary sugar, because it is better tolerated and has a smaller digestive effect, but he adds that one really can manage with sugar too.

About honey, Luka says he has never used it as the basis for his own gel. The reasons are price and logistics: the question is how to carry it and squeeze it out on the ride. If someone nevertheless wants to, they are free to, and for preparing one's own mixture he recommends looking in a sports shop for glucose or a similar carbohydrate powder.

About gummy candies, Luka admits that he himself uses them on some rides, without gels, when there are no special goals or big demands and when it is important to him only to take in carbohydrates. The key message is:

- as long as intake is kept at lower figures, up to about **60 grams per hour or less**, the ratios, forms and sources of carbohydrates **become less important**.

Josip concludes that the greatest advantage of gels is actually **packaging and practicality**. In a race a gel can be dealt with in the mouth in a hurry, while a sandwich is impossible to chew at pace. For recreational riders like him a gel can be "first aid", and the main source of energy can remain a sandwich or other food. Josip thus uses a gel when it happens that he eats nothing for two hours.

sections.subtitle: How nutrition protects against injuries and infections: the danger of prolonged energy deficit
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur talks about the consequences of prolonged energy deficit on bones and immunity
sections.content:
Josip returns to a claim Luka told him earlier: that injuries can be prevented through nutrition. He admits that it surprised him, because he had always associated injury prevention with stretching, warming up and the gym, not with food.

Luka gives context. That does not mean that someone who eats a quality piece of meat and risotto will be protected from falling off a bike. It is a topic he mentioned at the beginning, **relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S)**. He sees the biggest problem in athletes, and especially female athletes, burdened with appearance and body mass. For a good part of the time, for weeks and months, they train in a **serious energy deficit that is not structured or guided by an expert**. The comparison is as if someone set off toward Dubrovnik and did not fill the tank.

Luka lists the consequences of prolonged deficit:

- a greater chance that "bones start to crack",
- in women the loss of the cycle, which is a sign that the body is in chaos and shutting down functions that are not essential at that moment, and the bones can become "hollow". He mentions that even very young female athletes, around twenty years old, have come into such a state,
- susceptibility to infections,
- poorer quality of training,
- in the event of a collision or fall, a greater probability of a more serious fracture,
- in men, among other things, lower testosterone.

Luka stresses that the authors of the paper are also very clear in this regard. Calcium and vitamin D are also mentioned, but their role is **slightly inferior to ensuring adequate energy**. The same applies to immunity: instead of an emphasis on vitamins, the priority is to prevent too large a deficit. When training is very intense from day to day, or during stage races, one should try to replace everything that was expended, and if a deficit nevertheless occurs, keep it as small as possible.

Luka adds that the paper also contains several interesting tables comparing male and female cyclists, their average weight, power in watts and hours of training, and this in comparison with amateurs.

sections.subtitle: Daily carbohydrate intake: amateurs' most common mistake after training
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur warns that carbohydrate recommendations for heavy days can reach ten grams per kilogram
sections.content:
Luka stresses that carbohydrates must always be spoken about at the level of the whole day, not only during the ride. Recommendations are expressed in **grams per kilogram of body mass per day**, and the total figures require a lot of food: rice, pasta and the like.

This is where, Luka claims, amateurs most often go wrong. They copy professionals during training, and then after the ride they eat a big plate of pasta, which is their lunch, so **the rest of the day the diet "falls apart"**. Luka sees such cases all the time: athletes who seemingly do everything right, have a meal before and after training, but the rest of the day is a disaster and they are far from the goal. For days with about five hours of training, recommendations can go as high as **ten grams of carbohydrates per kilogram**, which is no joke. Some athletes in that case take in perhaps half of that, and the rest of the day eat a burger, pizza and drink beer with the explanation "I earned it". Luka says that sometimes something can be earned, but that this is not a strategy.

Josip shares his own experience. Last year he combined cycling and the gym, with five workouts a week, and sometimes seven or eight. He was in a deficit of about **three and a half to five thousand calories per week**. Sometimes he simply could not eat that amount of food, so he tried to take in as much protein as possible, and skimped on carbohydrates because he did not know this. He had no problems with injuries, but he had problems with fatigue.

Luka says this is a common picture in practice. Carbohydrates are stigmatized, and the fitness industry is much stronger than the sports nutrition industry. He adds that three times a week for half an hour to 45 minutes in the gym cannot be compared with three hours of cycling every day. He also admits that there are situations in which athletes really need to reduce the share of fat tissue, but what he sees in practice is often "warped". Sometimes authorities and trained coaches are to blame for this, and athletes then skip dinners or "smooth out" meals. Luka warned that this is very dangerous.

Josip adds that laypeople often latch onto some guru and follow him blindly. He was recently shocked to read that carbohydrates do not have to be an "enemy", but can help muscle growth, with an equal amount of protein. He also notes that a carbohydrate is not only bad food, but can also be a potato, a "top carbohydrate".

sections.subtitle: Luka at a gran fondo: glycogen compensation and preparation from Friday to race morning
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains glycogen compensation and nutrition preparation ahead of a gran fondo
sections.content:
Josip asks for a concrete example: Luka rode a gran fondo the other day, so he asks him what he ate before the race, what the evening before looked like and what he did afterward. Luka answers that the race was on Sunday.

Before the story about himself, he looks back at what scientific papers say about **glycogen compensation**: even 24 hours is enough, but it is more practical to do it over **two days**. It is easier to eat your fill over two days, on a satiety scale up to six or seven out of ten, than to try to cram everything in at once on the last day. The required intakes are very high, about **ten grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body mass per day**. For Luka, who is close to 90 kilograms, that would mean almost a kilogram of pure carbohydrates. He honestly says he did not take in that much, and everything also depends on the duration of the race, which he completed in about two and a half hours.

Luka's menu ahead of the race:

- **Friday:** a whole package (about 400 grams) of apple and sour cherry cake, along with half a kilogram of pasta which he and his partner shared. On the day before the race he tries to avoid fats and fiber,
- **Saturday:** a big portion of Čokolino, a lot of fruit and water replaced by **liquid calories** (Cedevita, juices). This is, he says, the most practical way to take in more carbohydrates without burdening digestion with a large volume of food. A jam sandwich and quite a lot of jelly also slipped in,
- **race morning:** an early wake-up, Čokolino Plus (he prefers it to the regular one) with low-fat milk, cake, half a liter of coffee, a handful of gummy candies half an hour before the start and a three-deciliter Red Bull. He adds that he occasionally takes caffeine in tablets too.

To Josip's question whether it depends on the importance of the race, Luka confirms that it definitely depends. He does not always do this, but when he has triathlete clients before the season, he thinks about whether it makes sense to do a super compensation. If an important training session of four to five hours follows over the weekend, it makes sense to raise carbohydrates on Friday, but not with french fries and fried squid, but, for example, with seafood risotto.

sections.subtitle: Two hundred grams in 2:42, empty legs near the end, and recovery with bolognese, fruit and cakes
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur describes intake during the race and how his legs got "clogged" in the last kilometers
sections.content:
During the race itself, Luka had about 120 people around him. In the bottles he had carbohydrates: in one about 7 deciliters, in the other half a liter. In addition he took six gels, of which he ate five, and he also used the refreshment at the first station. When he later calculated, in **two hours and 42 minutes he took in about 200 grams of carbohydrates**.

To Josip's question whether that was enough for him, Luka honestly answers: „I burned out.“ In the last twenty or so kilometers part of the group began to feel their legs. A larger group caught up with them near the end and he managed to do a sprint, but his legs were quite clogged for the last five to six kilometers. He thinks he did not pace himself best and that it would not necessarily have helped even if he had taken in more, because **it is not always about carbohydrates, but also about form**.

Luka also tells an anecdote from the race. His partner arrived only a few seconds behind him. He and a colleague were riding the last climb, and a group appeared behind them. According to his telling, part of that crew, somewhere between 70th and 100th place, was not quite fair, because his partner with several colleagues had been pulling a fairly large group, so she told them that they should also pitch in a bit. Josip recalls that she took a podium at that race a few years ago, and maybe even first place.

Recovery after the race was not left out:

- they immediately ate the bolognese that was handed out at lunch, with bread and potatoes with meat,
- in a hurry he ate forest fruit, which is his "equivalent" of what professionals get after a stage,
- then at her parents', because it was her birthday, there was cake, pastries and croissants.

Luka adds that he used himself up, and next weekend a new race awaits him and additional training.

sections.subtitle: Recovery when a new demanding training follows: large amounts of food by plan
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains how many carbohydrates are needed to recover glycogen before a new hard training session
sections.content:
On the basis of his example, Luka concludes what this means for the average recreational rider. When someone finishes a more intense training session, race or gran fondo, and knows that **a new demanding training session awaits them in two or three days**, strong amounts of food and carbohydrates are needed. Those amounts should be taken in in a targeted and planned way.

In the paper this is written in several places. The authors also looked at an intake of **13 grams of carbohydrates per kilogram of body mass**, and even that in some situations was not enough for glycogen stores to be completely replenished within 24 hours, to a certain extent. Luka says he does not want to bore people with chemistry and details about muscle dry matter, but stresses that these are **very high stakes**. That is important if someone has more serious ambitions and if after a harder training session, race or brevet a new task awaits them in a few days.

Josip follows up with his own experience. On cycling trips and multi-day rides he always tried to make the dinner after the ride as rich in carbohydrates as possible, so that the body could recover more easily and faster.

sections.subtitle: How to maintain muscle mass: proteins, strength training and bike packing
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains that for preserving muscle the most important thing is total daily protein intake
sections.content:
Josip reads a question from viewer Marin Milardović: how to maintain muscle mass most safely, that is, to lose only fat tissue, in races or on bike packing.

Luka first separates the worlds of cycling. It is not in everyone's interest to have a big biceps or shoulders, and there is a reason why most better cyclists are quite slim in the upper body. To maintain or increase muscle mass an **adequate stimulus** is needed, which is the job of kinesiologists and as a rule comes down to strength training, that is, lifting heavy things. In addition, an adequate amount of protein is needed.

Luka repeats that there is no evidence that something bad will happen if proteins are not taken in during the ride itself, even when it lasts six or seven hours. As fuel for performance they do not help, and for preserving muscle and for recovery the key is **total daily protein intake**. For a bike packer this means that it is practical to cover part of the protein with breakfast, and the rest in the evening in a tent, hotel or restaurant with meat, fish and eggs. Protein bars will probably not harm him, because bike packing is not the same as wanting to finish in the top 10 percent of a gran fondo.

Luka also gives an example: someone spends a month bike packing around Europe, returns to the gym and cannot lift the same weight on the bench, and his arms have "dried out". That is normal, because for a month he did not load the muscles as before. If muscles could be maintained by nutrition alone, Luka says jokingly, "all our politicians would be bodybuilders". The recommendation is that you nevertheless eat some protein for the rest of the day. According to his words, **1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body mass** is quite enough even for muscle growth, and with the amount of food cyclists eat this figure is easy to exceed.

Josip tells how a friend recently contacted him who is going bike packing for the first time, for five to seven days, and asked whether he should do strength exercises. Josip thinks he doesn't need to, because he will ride all day and is unlikely to lose much in those few days. Luka says he is not a kinesiologist and does not feel competent in that, but does not believe that five days would change anything significant, with a joke about a "biceps at the rest stop". Josip then announces that, since an hour and fifteen minutes have passed, a few more viewer questions will go through before the conclusion.

iterations.theme: Viewer questions: nutrition at a brevet, everyday nutrition, supplements (beetroot, caffeine, creatine), and the conclusion and end of the podcast

sections.subtitle: Eggs and bacon at a brevet: why Luka Batur would not reach for that sandwich
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur comments on egg and bacon sandwiches as a choice for a brevet
sections.content:
Josip moves on to the viewers' questions, and the first relates to nutrition at brevets. The viewer asks what to eat the day before and during the ride and what is best to drink. During brevets he himself eats sandwiches with eggs and bacon and various chocolate bars, and drinks water from a bottle. He is also interested in how much magnesium to take and when: before, during or after the ride.

**Luka Batur** first stresses that he has already given most of the answers in the conversation. What jumps out at him most are the eggs and bacon, which he would not choose as a first choice, for reasons he has already explained:

- fats and proteins slow gastric emptying,
- fats do not contribute to total energy expenditure in the way the athlete needs during the ride,
- even the leanest individuals have enough fat that will be used during training and the race, so in that sense there is no need to worry.

According to Batur it is a pity that fats take the place of carbohydrates. He also admits that a brevet is not the same as a race. If the rider feels good, there is no reason to change in a panic, but he would reduce the emphasis on speck and pancetta and turn to milder options, for example slices of ham or a light spread. With recreational riders who ride a brevet without too great ambitions he would be more relaxed than before a gran fondo or an event with more serious goals.

### Own experience: Zagreb – Šibenik

Batur tells that three or four years ago he went by bike from Zagreb to Šibenik. He did not have a sandwich: he thought he had eaten two strudels and drunk half a liter of Coke, and along the way bars, carbohydrates and gummy candies kept him going. On the stretch from Gračac to Knin he was probably in more serious dehydration, and gummy and jelly candies and three deciliters of water saved him. He would not go on such tours as if a platter of food at a wedding or on Christmas Eve lay ahead of him, he says, something that is not his first option.

### Magnesium: better in the evening

About magnesium supplements Batur says that quite a few myths circulate:

- magnesium losses through sweating are very small, almost non-existent,
- there is no recommendation for magnesium intake during activity,
- most products contain poor forms, such as oxides and carbonates, which are poorly absorbed. Of the stated 400 milligrams the body would use only about three percent,
- there is also the possibility of an oxidative effect.

That is why he would not drink magnesium either before or during activity. He himself takes it in the evening, in the form of glycinate. Josip adds that he, too, during rides sometimes took glycine tablets preventively. Batur answers that one feels better in the head that way, which is fine, but that by all accounts it has no real effect.

sections.subtitle: Sweet cravings: more carbohydrates through the day instead of chocolate by the spoon
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur describes a typical Sunday of the average Croatian cyclist after a ride
sections.content:
The next question comes from a viewer who follows Batur's posts on Instagram. He wants to know how to reconcile nutrition with all life's obligations and hobbies, and what to do about the feeling that he needs something sweet, say a piece of chocolate.

**Luka Batur** says he does such consultations daily, both with athletes and with recreational riders. He is sorry that sweet is often stigmatized, because in his opinion it is perfectly fine to have a desire for something sweet. But in people who do sports, especially more intensely, a good part of the craving for sweets is often a consequence of a lack of carbohydrates in the diet.

### The classic Sunday of the average cyclist

Batur describes a scenario he often sees. The cyclist comes back from the ride, the first thing is a beer, and then a barbecue or stuffed fatty pork loin appears on the table. Half a kilo of meat is eaten, maybe one potato, which is the equivalent of about 50 grams of carbohydrates, and with it a slice of bread. In the afternoon or evening follows a whole Milka Oreo or Nutella by the spoon. Few carbohydrates have been taken in, and fats about 50 percent more than needed, so that cyclist, as he says, „stays fat and slow.”

Batur's advice is that carbohydrates be thickened up through the day:

- **fruit** is the simplest source, and people eat too little of it,
- squeezed juice is a good option, and even when there is no time an orange juice can be bought,
- where possible, every day one should have a portion of polenta, rice, barley, pasta or potatoes.

In some cases, he says, he literally gives people permission to eat carbohydrates. It is paradoxical to him that someone is afraid of carbohydrates, but is not afraid of chocolate. He immediately adds that he does not want his words taken out of context: food and chocolate do not have to be „earned” with training. But if the goal is to be faster and recover better, the level of carbohydrates must be at the appropriate level.

At the household level he suggests that days with harder training be filled with pasta, rice or lasagna, and roasts and barbecues be left for days when it is not so important. For concrete advice to the viewer he admits that he lacks context. He would need about 45 minutes to get acquainted with someone's everyday life, and only then can he turn it into concrete steps, for example one additional banana, more bread with dinner, or a glass of squeezed juice when there is no time.

sections.subtitle: Gels, bars, gummy candies: combining carbohydrate sources on a long ride
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains the importance of testing different gels and flavors in training
sections.content:
Josip relays a question from a viewer from Serbia who is preparing for his first ride of eight and a half hours. He wants to know how many different carbohydrate sources he can use and whether it is better for the stomach to stick to two or three sources or whether there can be more.

Before that, Josip also mentions a question about which energy bar Hrvoje Jurić recommends. **Luka Batur** tries to remember who this is about, asks whether it is the gentleman who rode a certain route by bike, but in the end admits that he does not know what he recommends.

### Combining is welcome

Batur explains that if the viewer by „source” means form, that is, liquid, gel, bar or gummy candies, he can freely combine sources. Moreover, he recommends it, so that flavor fatigue does not occur. On a long ride that is not a race there is room for personal preferences, but it still should be narrowed down a little. He admits that he himself would most like to have „everything” in his pocket, even a sandwich.

To clients he advises to try different products in practice:

- there are some twenty different kinds of gels, of which some may stink, be sour, bitter or too sweet,
- one should try products from several manufacturers and several brands,
- only when you know what suits you is it possible to put together combinations.

### The client with a table

Batur tells an anecdote about a client who made an „old school” table, without Excel. He tried gels, wrote them down and ranked them by texture and taste, and in the end narrowed the choice to a few products, mathematically pedantic, and said: this is my choice, I stick to it.

Josip adds that this is always an individual matter, because for one person the taste won't suit, and for another the texture, even when someone tells him the product is the best in the world. That is why he always tells people to try new products on a relaxed training ride, so they know how they react when the important thing comes. Batur completely agrees.

sections.subtitle: Lamb or veal? A humorous question that the nutritionist does not answer with meat
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur jokingly gives his stance on lamb, veal and fish
sections.content:
To end the viewers' questions, Josip reads a humorous question: what is better for cyclists, lamb from the spit or veal under the peka? He himself roots for grilled lamb chops, which he considers „numero uno.”

**Luka Batur** immediately announces that he will come across as a „hick.” From his parts, veal under the peka is well known, but he does not know since when Dalmatia became a land of lamb and not of fish. He admits that he is subjective: his father is a fisherman, and he himself has a professional qualification for commercial fishing. He could, he jokes, have put the diploma ahead of the master's in nutrition. He honestly says he would not eat either one or the other because he doesn't like it. In his defense he adds that his girlfriend doesn't like chicken and that lately he hardly eats white meat at all. Josip stays with his view: chops.

After that Josip sums up that through the conversation they have already gone through amateurs' misconceptions when copying professionals and the organization of nutrition, and returns to the question about the mention of forest fruit after the race and beetroot.

sections.subtitle: Beetroot and nitrates: the economy that helps amateurs the most
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur explains how nitrates from beetroot juice improve economy
sections.content:
Josip asks why beetroot is so popular. **Luka Batur** explains that it is a supplement, and the key is nitrates. Oxygen is needed for the muscle to work and for fuel to burn, and nitrates from beetroot juice make it possible to get more work from the same amount of oxygen. Scientists call this economy, so with beetroot juice one can be faster and do more work.

### The better trained, the smaller the effect

For amateurs this is, he says, actually good news. Research shows that beetroot works less the better trained the athlete is. Batur mentions a group with a very high VO2 max, above 65, in which the effect is not so pronounced. Either through training they have reached the ceiling of adaptations so this no longer makes a significant difference, or it is something that is not yet known. In any case, beetroot can help better economy and efficiency of performance, and in already very fit athletes it will probably not have a significant effect.

Batur himself drinks beetroot juice a couple of days before an important race, and through the week he will drink it before a half Ironman as well. If someone is hungry, he advises, they should not drink it.

### How much and when?

To Josip's question about amount and timing Batur answers that we are talking about around **half a liter of beetroot juice per day for 3 to 4 days**, even up to 7 days before the main event, race or training. This is not entirely practical, and products of this kind can also be unacceptable in price.

sections.subtitle: Caffeine, creatine, beta alanine and bicarbonate: what is worth it and what is not for everyone
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur lists supplements and explains for whom creatine makes sense
sections.content:
The next topic is a short overview of supplements, which Batur prepared in notes. Josip adds that, along with the paper, he will leave a link.

### Caffeine

Caffeine, says **Luka Batur**, definitely reduces the perception of fatigue. He mostly recommends it, but not in the afternoon hours, so that it does not affect sleep. It can be taken in the form of tablets, coffee or Red Bull, and the recommended amount is **3 to 6 milligrams per kilogram of body mass**, in the first part of the day.

### Creatine

There is a lot of discussion about creatine. Batur states who probably should not take it:

- the crowd that hits steady watts for five to six hours, without many jumps, sprints and breakaways, because for them the ratio of mass to power matters, and creatine brings a slight increase in mass of half a kilo to a kilo (not in everyone),
- riders who want to be as light as possible on climbs.

Where could he recommend it? Where there are quick explosive actions, for example in XC and on mountain bike races. For sprinter teams, he says, it makes sense because they are protected from the influence of mass, and an average of about 150 watts is ridden for five hours and then a sprint. For recreational riders for whom half a kilo up or down is not decisive, creatine can help with recovery, glycogen synthesis and adaptations. If someone trains or most of their races are steadily under a clenched head, it can even be counterproductive.

### Beta alanine and bicarbonate

**Beta alanine** neutralizes H+ ions (as he himself says, the term „lactic acid” is not correct) and is useful for submaximal intervals. This applies to the crowd that trains in a structured way and has a plan with regular intervals. For those who just go out riding it makes no sense. Definitely a „thumbs up” if a coach is involved.

**Baking soda** can be extremely problematic. Serious gastro problems can occur, including pronounced diarrhea. Some teams also use ready-made commercial systems with bicarbonate, but they are very expensive so Batur would not recommend them.

### Summary for more serious recreational riders

For a somewhat more serious crowd Batur definitely recommends caffeine, and beta alanine and creatine can be tried. Occasionally it wouldn't hurt to enrich the diet with beetroot juice.

sections.subtitle: Should there be a break from coffee in winter? Caffeine, habit and the time of the last cup
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur answers a question about a break from caffeine and the latest time of intake
sections.content:
Josip mentions that he read or heard somewhere that some professional cyclists stop caffeine for a month in winter so that it works at full strength again at the start of the season. He wants to know whether that makes sense.

**Luka Batur** answers that, according to the research he knows, the crowd that constantly drinks coffee and the like is asked whether it is less sensitive because of habit. According to what can be seen, there is no excessive reason for a break, and the effect will not disappear just because caffeine is used for a long time. If athletes nevertheless take a break, it is probably because of side effects, such as jitters, anxiety or poorer sleep quality. By his estimate it is also more likely that outside the season there is no need for an additional boost in training. To clients' question whether they must give up coffee so that it works better later, he therefore answers that probably not.

### The last train: 14 to 15 o'clock

The timing of intake is more important. Batur stresses that caffeine should be removed from the late afternoon hours, because he does not want to affect the quality of sleep. Athletes sometimes tell him they drank their last coffee at 17 or 18 o'clock or took a tablet before training, and they should not be doing that. His suggestion is **the last train somewhere around 14 or 15 o'clock**.

Josip is surprised because he himself can drink coffee at 17 or 18 o'clock, and he considered that the last train. Batur explains that caffeine has a half-life of three to four hours and that it depends on the amount. One cup of coffee later in the afternoon will probably not be a problem, but with larger doses it is different:

- 200 to 300 milligrams of caffeine is equivalent to roughly four to five Red Bulls or two to three capsules,
- one espresso has about 60 to 80 milligrams,
- such doses are recommended to be removed up to nine hours before sleep.

The reason is simple: the next day you need to wake up functional and do a new training session or go to work.

sections.subtitle: Conclusion: do not copy professionals and look at nutrition across the whole day
sections.screenshot_description: Luka Batur sums up the podcast's key messages about total daily intake and recovery
sections.content:
Josip asks for the conclusion of the conversation, and **Luka Batur** announces that he will be quick and sums up the messages:

- **Do not imitate professionals** in the amount of carbohydrates per hour just because someone thinks they will be a „big shot” if they eat half a kilo of sugar an hour.
- **The rest of the day is equally important.** It is worth taking care of the afternoon meal and dinner, just as much as of the Čokolino before training. Total daily intake, the amount and quality of food, is key for recovery. If training awaits you the next day, the fact that you ate 120 grams per hour over two hours is not an indicator that your nutrition is good in general, nor in the rest of the day.
- **Energy is the priority.** For injuries and infections, an adequate supply of energy takes precedence over antioxidants, vitamin C and similar supplements.

### Antioxidants and cherry juice

Batur warns about antioxidant tablets in doses above normal physiological ones, which are not recommended because they can blunt adaptations to training. As an example he cites the pink drink that professionals are pushed into their hands after a stage, cherry juice, that is, sour cherry juice, which is rich in antioxidants. He wonders why they give it to them if too large a dose can put a „lid” on adaptations. He answers that at the Tour nobody is working on adaptations: the goal is to recover as soon as possible because a new race follows the next day. He suspects they do the same during preparations, when it is in their interest to stimulate adaptations so they do not want to shut them down with supplements.

### Beer after the ride

Batur admits that he did not answer the question about beer and pizza. One beer is probably not a problem and will not kill anyone. But alcohol inhibits glycogen synthesis, and to a greater extent can also dehydrate. If someone claims they want to be fast and recover as well as possible, and says it with a beer in hand, he would „be a bit suspicious.” He does not want to stigmatize anyone and admits that there are immeasurably better athletes who drink beer, but he thinks they are good despite it, not because of it. The question is what would have happened if they had first done recovery with juice or something more concrete.

About Josip's examples of Bayern footballers and the Croatian national team who drink beer and eat pizza after victories, Batur doubts that alcohol is part of the prescribed recovery. It is more likely that the camera caught a moment of celebration after the match. If the goals are weight, minutes or bigger and more ambitious training, one wants to devote oneself to details, and alcohol and overly heavy food in the first hours after a gran fondo or a harder training session are not the best friends.

sections.subtitle: Čokolino Friday and farewell: an invitation to viewers to comment and to collaborate with Luka
sections.screenshot_description: Josip and Luka Batur in the closing part of the podcast with a joke about Čokolino Friday
sections.content:
To close, Josip announces that in the description he will leave a link to the scientific paper that was discussed, for those who are interested in more. He invites viewers to mention Luka Batur in the comments. He suggested to him that over some period of time, monthly or quarterly, he record a video about nutrition science for the biciklizam.net channel or open his own channel. He thinks that would be very useful, so he asks viewers to „attack” him in the comments, so that he would not have to open fake profiles.

Batur jokes that it could be „Čokolino Friday”, and Josip follows up on that idea. Batur immediately clarifies that Podravka does not sponsor him, but that he is open to collaboration.

Josip invites viewers to look at Batur's links, website and Instagram, if they have questions for him or want a collaboration, and to subscribe to the channel. To those interested in more nutrition science he recommends also watching the previous video. The podcast ends with a mutual farewell, and Josip adds at the end that the batteries are switching off.
